books.title: Nutmeg's Stormy Barn

pages.text: Nutmeg has a farm with a red barn. Her corn is tall, and the first stars are out.
pages.prompt: What can Nutmeg see on her farm?

pages.text: Dark clouds start to form. A storm is coming! Nutmeg must get her corn to the barn.
A small bird chirps on the fence. Her nest is torn, and she cannot fly far.
pages.prompt: What is wrong with the bird?

pages.text: Nutmeg turns back. She lifts the bird and runs for the barn door. Thunder roars in the dark.
pages.prompt: What does Nutmeg choose to do first?

pages.text: Morning comes. Some of the corn is torn, but the bird chirps on the porch. Nutmeg smiles. A farm is more than corn.

books.title: Panda-Cake's Puddle Party

pages.text: It is a rainy day, and Ted-E-Bear is not happy. His sunny picnic will have to wait.
Panda-Cake has a little idea. She sets a table by the window with an apple cake.
Ted looks out. There is a puddle in the middle of the path, and a duckling is paddling in it.
"That looks funny!" says Ted. They run out and jump in the puddle. Splash! They giggle.
They come in muddy and happy, and share the apple cake. A rainy day can be a jolly day too.

books.title: Polly Roger and the Red Wings of Copán

pages.text: Rosa is an exchange student at Wise Owl's school. She is from Honduras. Today, she is taking her friend Polly Roger home.
They fly over green hills. "In Honduras, we call a red macaw a guara roja," says Rosa. "I am one, and so are you!"
pages.prompt: What do people in Honduras call a red macaw?

pages.text: Rosa leads Polly to Copán. Long ago, the Maya people built this city from stone. Polly stops. "Look! A stone bird is peeking at me!"
"Maya carvers made macaws in stone," Rosa says. "But real macaws nearly vanished from this valley. Then people started helping."
pages.prompt: What nearly vanished from the valley?

pages.text: Rosa shows Polly a neat nest box high in a tree. Two chicks are peeping inside. "We are coming back," Rosa says.
pages.prompt: How did people help the macaws?

pages.text: At sunset, they eat a warm baleada together. Red wings are flying over the old stones. Polly smiles. "This is the best treasure."
pages.prompt: What does Polly call the best treasure?

quiz2.question: Why do people put nest boxes in the trees?
quiz2.answer: To help the macaws come back to the valley

books.title: Rosa's Copán Report

pages.text: My name is Rosa, and I am an exchange student from Honduras. My teacher asked me to tell the class about my home. I chose Copán, because its history and its birds belong together.

Copán is in western Honduras, close to the border with Guatemala. More than a thousand years ago, it was a great Maya city. In 1980, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, so people around the world now help to protect it.

The most famous place in Copán is the Hieroglyphic Stairway. Maya carvers covered its stone steps with more than a thousand glyphs. It is the longest Maya text that we know. Reading it is like opening a history book made of stone.
Macaws mattered to the Maya of Copán. Carvers shaped macaw heads for the ball court, and the name of the city's first ruler includes the word for macaw. These birds were part of the city's identity.
pages.prompt: How do we know macaws mattered?

pages.text: Scarlet macaws nest in holes high in tall trees. A female usually lays two to four eggs, and the chicks hatch blind and without feathers. Fruit and nuts are the main foods of these birds, and they can live for decades.

Scarlet macaws almost disappeared from the valley. Then people began to build nests, watch the chicks and teach visitors. Now macaws fly over Copán again. My report has one question for you: what is worth protecting where you live?

quiz.answer: More than a thousand carved glyphs

quiz2.question: How did people help the macaws return?
quiz2.answer: They built nests, watched the chicks and taught visitors

quiz3.question: Why are history and birds linked at Copán?
quiz3.answer: The Maya carved macaws and valued them, and macaws live in the valley today

books.title: Nutmeg and the Tree That Wouldn’t Come

pages.text: The week before Christmas, Nutmeg shook the wooden star out of her mitten drawer. It had a dent in one point where she had dropped it when she was small. She put the red loop round her wrist.

“I’ve found our tree!” she called to Corgi. “It’s just the right size. This year even I can reach the top.” Out they went with the library’s little red cart. The wheels made two neat lines in the snow.
The fir stood in a wooden barrel behind the library. It smelled of cold rain and pine. One branch stuck straight out, like a paw waiting to shake. “Ready, fir?” said Nutmeg.
Corgi held the cart steady. Nutmeg took hold of the barrel. They counted to three. The cart bumped. The snow slipped. The barrel stayed exactly where it was.
“Perhaps it’s frozen to the ground,” said Corgi. He swept away the loose snow with one paw. Nutmeg brushed a little farther. Under the rim of the barrel, something brown curved into the earth.
It was a root. It had slipped out through a split in the wood. In the time it took Nutmeg to grow out of two pairs of mittens, the little fir had gone and planted itself.
Nutmeg let go of the barrel. “The whole square is waiting for this tree,” she said. She looked up at the green tips. She looked down at the little root. She put the star back in her pocket.

They walked round to the square. Professor Hooten was putting a low bench by the noticeboard. Panda-Cake had brought a tin of star biscuits. In the middle of the square was a big, swept circle. It looked terribly empty.
“The fir has roots,” Nutmeg told them. “I told everybody there would be a tree.” She rubbed the dent in her star through her pocket. Hooten set the bench down and listened.
“We could make one out of broom handles,” said Corgi. He crossed two brooms and put his tail through the middle. Nutmeg laughed in spite of herself. Then both brooms slid over with a clack.
Nutmeg looked from the empty square to the empty cart. “We were going to bring the tree to the party,” she said. She touched the cart’s cold handle. “What if the party could come to the tree?”

They brought Hooten to see the garden. He liked the fir’s crooked branch. He liked the long wall that kept off the wind. Then he pointed to the stone step at the front. “How will we get my bench down that?”

Corgi disappeared round the corner. A moment later his ears popped up on the other side of the garden gate. “There’s a lane back here,” he called. Nutmeg could just see his tail between two tall snowbanks.

The lane was wide enough for the cart, if they cleared the snow. Scritch went Hooten’s shovel. Shush went Nutmeg’s broom. Corgi tried to help with his tail. “You’re sweeping it straight at me,” said Nutmeg.

Hooten walked the whole lane with the loaded cart. It rolled through the gate without a bump. Nutmeg put fallen pinecones along the edge. Corgi carried one at a time, very carefully, as if each one were an egg.
Back in the square, somebody had put up a long paper chain. Nutmeg and Corgi each took an end. They had nearly reached the garden when the wind caught the middle.
Rip! The chain came apart. A red loop landed over Corgi’s nose. Nutmeg picked up three muddy loops and sat very still. For a moment she wished she had stayed home with her mittens.

Then Panda-Cake came round the corner with his biscuit tin. He sat down right there in the snow. “Did you know a broken star biscuit still tastes like cinnamon?” he said, and gave Nutmeg the bigger piece.
Nutmeg took a bite. “A little piece of paper chain will still look nice, too.” They rescued the dry parts. The longest went on the library door, the shortest on the back of Hooten’s bench.

Then Nutmeg walked back to the square. By now there were neighbours in hats and boots, standing round the empty circle. She climbed onto the low step. “Our Christmas tree has settled in,” she said. “Follow my pinecones.”
The smallest neighbour spotted the next pinecone and hurried ahead. The slowest took Hooten’s arm. One by one they came through the garden gate. No one had to climb the stone step.

The fir was quite small with everyone around it. Nutmeg found she could reach the crooked branch without standing on tiptoe. She pulled the star out of her pocket and slipped its red loop over the green needles.

At first the wooden star looked very plain. Then Hooten switched on the garden lantern. A little light caught in the dent. Panda-Cake opened his tin. Somebody began a song, and Nutmeg knew the second line.

Later, when only the little footprints were left, Nutmeg came back for her cart. A dusting of snow lay on the branch above the star. “See you tomorrow, fir,” she said. And she left the star just where it was.

books.title: Vincent Van Mouse and the Christmas Shadow Show

pages.text: Vincent Van Mouse had painted six chimneys, four puddles and the little bakery door. He paused over a roof that he knew by heart. His own house had just enough room for a crooked chimney and a mouse.

The picture was for the library’s Christmas window. Tonight, when the snow made the streets go blue, everyone would come to see it. Vincent imagined them finding their houses. He wondered who would spot his first.

Panda-Cake brought a tin of biscuits for the audience. “There’s a bit of red on your nose,” he told him. Vincent rubbed his cheek. “Other side.” He rubbed his chin. Panda-Cake handed him a clean rag, which he forgot to use.
Together they lifted the long painting. “I’ll hold this end,” said Panda-Cake. “You hold yours.” Vincent trotted backwards towards the window. The picture sagged in the middle, like a washing line.
Professor Hooten opened the hall door to bring in the chairs. Cold air rushed past him. The small paper stars on the shelf trembled. Then the great sheet of painted paper gave a shiver of its own.
“Hold it there!” cried Vincent. He gripped his end with both paws. Panda-Cake held his. The gust pushed the middle up and over the corner of the window latch.
Rrrrip. A rip ran down the Christmas street, stopping just above the bottom edge. Half of Vincent’s chimney folded back. He could see Panda-Cake through the hole where his house ought to have been.

Hooten shut the door. “That was a big gust,” he said softly. Vincent put the painting on the table. He tried to press the chimney flat. His paw was shaking, so Panda-Cake set the rag beside him and waited.

They tried to mend the rip from behind. The two sides almost met. But the paint had stuck to the latch and come away, leaving a white stripe down the wall of Vincent’s house. He tucked his brush inside his apron.
Outside, one child stood on tiptoe to peer through the glass. Another was brushing snow off the window ledge with a mitten. Vincent could see them. He slid down in his chair so they couldn’t see him.
Panda-Cake took a cardboard star from the shelf. “We could put a star over the white bit.” The desk lamp was already on. When he picked up the star, its shadow swept over the wall.
“Hold it there,” said Vincent. This time he said it very quietly. He watched the star grow when Panda-Cake moved it towards the lamp. When he moved back, it shrank. He climbed out of his chair.
Vincent snipped round the torn flap and lifted it. On the wall, the scrap became a steep little roof. He tipped it sideways, and there was his crooked chimney. “There you are,” he said.

“Hooten, may we borrow a sheet?” asked Vincent. “And could the chairs face this way?” He pointed away from the window, towards the warm end of the hall, where two low bookcases stood with a gap between them.

Hooten clipped a plain sheet to two tall poles behind the bookcases and set the lamp on a table behind it. Panda-Cake walked round to the front. Vincent lifted his roof. A house popped up on the sheet. “I can see it from here!” he called.
Vincent took his little scissors. From the snowy strip below the rip, he snipped a new row of roofs. Panda-Cake cut a cardboard squirrel with a parcel under its arm.

The squirrel looked very fine from the front, until Panda-Cake tried to make it walk. Its parcel bumped a roof. Its tail went up a chimney. “That’s the wrong way home,” said Vincent, laughing for the first time since the rip.

They tried again. This time the squirrel stood farther from the lamp, beside the sheet. Small enough! It trotted down the street between the roofs. Vincent practised making the star rise. Panda-Cake practised three little taps.

Hooten went out to the waiting children. “The Christmas picture is ready,” he said. “Come inside and find a chair.” Behind the sheet, Vincent heard boots tapping and two last chairs scraping along the floor.
Panda-Cake tapped his spoon on the biscuit tin. Ting. Ting. Ting. The hall went quiet. Vincent raised the little street. On the sheet, rooftops grew out of a pool of gold.
A squirrel travelled from house to house. At the last door, she set down her parcel and knocked. Then up came the star. A small voice in the front row whispered, “That’s Vincent’s chimney.”

Vincent almost forgot to move the star. He had thought his chimney was ruined. Here it was, as crooked as ever, big enough for the whole room to see. He held the star steady while the audience clapped.

Afterwards the children took turns with the puppets. One made the squirrel as big as a house. One put the star in the squirrel’s paws. Panda-Cake opened the biscuit tin. Vincent looked down and found another red spot on his apron.

He turned off the lamp and carried the crooked little house to the window. Outside, the snow had stopped. The silhouette sat on the sill beside the last biscuit. Vincent licked a crumb off his paw. “Good night, little house.”

books.title: One More Story Before Santa

pages.text:
On Christmas Eve, Coop-Accino put three star biscuits on a blue plate. One had a bent point.

“That one looks like it’s waving,” she said. She turned it so it waved at the door.

Cluck O’Clock poured a glass of milk. The glass made a tiny clink when he set it down.

“I’d hear that from upstairs,” he said.

“You can hear a biscuit break from upstairs,” said Coop-Accino.

“I’ll listen,” said Cluck. “You look.”

“And if one of us sees Santa, we wake the other.”

They tapped wingtips over the plate. It was a very quiet sort of promise.

On the stairs, Coop stopped. She could see the snow through the landing window, but the dark glass showed mostly her own beak.

“How will he know which house is ours?”

Hen-Berry came up with the bedtime book tucked under her wing.

“One more story,” said Cluck. “A short one. We’ve got a lot of listening to do.”

“And looking,” said Coop.

Hen-Berry sat between their beds and opened the book.

“Once there was a little mouse who moved into a house with no chimney.”

“None at all?” asked Coop.

“A drainpipe,” said Hen-Berry. “And a very fine front door.”
“On Christmas Eve, the mouse drew a chimney on a piece of paper. She stuck it to the door. Then she went down the path to see how it looked.”
“She couldn’t see the paper. She couldn’t even see the door. So she fetched a little lamp and put it in the front window. From the end of the path, she could see the whole window shining.”

“Did anyone come?” asked Cluck.

“Her grandad did,” said Hen-Berry. “He’d walked up and down twice looking for the right house.”

Coop shut the book with one wing. “We have a little lamp.”

Hen-Berry switched on the lamp by the front door. Back upstairs, she showed them the small patch of gold it made on the snow.

“We can keep an eye on that,” said Coop.

Hen-Berry tucked them in and left the door ajar.

“Eyes open,” whispered Coop.

“Ears open,” whispered Cluck.

For a while, all he could hear was Coop trying to breathe quietly.

Clink.

Cluck sat straight up. “The milk glass!”

Clink.

The sound was coming from somewhere much closer than the kitchen.

Coop pointed to the bedside table. The chain of Cluck’s watch was tapping the side of the brass bed as he wriggled.

He tucked the chain under the watch. “That’s one thing we’ve caught.”

“Antlers!” said Coop.

Two dark points poked into the patch of gold. She held the curtain back. The points went down and came up again.

“There. Did you see?”

Cluck squinted. A lump of snow slid off one point.

“That’s the shrub by the step,” he said.

“I know,” said Coop. “I was just seeing if you knew.”

The snow grew thick. It covered the shrub, then hid the fence. Coop let the curtain fall.

“Eyes open?” Cluck asked.

“Just resting them,” she said.

For a little while neither twin spoke. Then the snow thinned and a strip of sky opened above the trees.

Cluck saw something curved pass through it.
He touched Coop’s wing. She lifted the edge of the curtain just as four small shapes crossed the gap. In front, two sets of antlers tipped up, then two more.
Cluck leaned sideways to look again. The bit he’d seen curved up at the front, like the runner on their little sled. A fine line joined it to the shapes ahead.

Then the snow closed over the gap. Coop pressed her beak to the window and left a little round mark in the mist.

“Did you see where they went?”

“Past the trees, I think.”

“I saw the runners,” said Cluck.

“I saw the reindeer,” said Coop.

They looked at each other, then up at the empty sky. Between them, they had almost the whole thing.

From his bed, Cluck could still see the patch of gold by the step.

“Should we go down and check the plate?”

Coop thought about it. Then she pulled her quilt up to her beak. “Morning.”

Cluck turned his pillow over to the cool side.

“Tell me your bit in the morning?” he asked.

“If you tell me yours.”

This time their wingtips didn’t quite reach.

“Eyes open?” whispered Cluck.

Coop’s eyes had slipped shut.

“Ears open,” she whispered back.

Down by the step, snow fell through the little patch of gold.

books.title: The Last Parcel Under the Tree

pages.text:
Christmas morning turned the library steps pink.

Ted-E-Bear stamped the snow off his boots. Inside, Professor Hooten was putting an extra cup on the table. Every chair had a cup beside it already.

“Who’s that for?” asked Ted.

“We might need it,” said Hooten.

Corgi-on-the-Cob came skidding up the path with a parcel under his chin.

“Did I miss the presents?”

“You missed a chance to walk slowly,” said Ted.

Corgi shook snow out of his ears. A whole lump dropped down the back of Ted’s scarf.

Panda-Cake carried in a warm jug of cocoa. Hooten pulled the chairs into a ring around the paper tree they’d made for the hall.

“A little room by the door, please,” Hooten said.

Corgi moved his chair. Then he moved it back a tiny bit. From there he could see his parcel.

Corgi’s gift from Ted was a red ball with a white stripe. Corgi rolled it along his nose and caught it under his chin.

“I can do three in a row,” he said.

The ball rolled behind the tree on the second go.

Ted opened Corgi’s gift. It was a yellow notebook with a pencil tucked through a loop. The first page was quite clean, except for one sandy paw print.

“That’s so you know which way up it goes,” said Corgi.

Ted decided to leave the print right where it was.

Panda-Cake tried on his new green oven mitts. He could pick up the warm jug with them, but he couldn’t pick up a single biscuit.

He held the plate for Corgi instead.

When the paper had been gathered and folded, Hooten said, “That’s the presents opened.”

Ted bent to get the red ball from behind the tree. Something blue caught his eye under the lowest branch.

It was a cord, tied around a plain brown box. A tag stuck out from the knot.

“Wait,” Ted said. “There’s one left.”

Corgi put his nose right up to the tag. Ted turned it so they could both see.

It said, “For whoever gets there last.”

“That’s me,” said Corgi. “I was the last one through the door.”

Ted looked at the cup without a chair.

“You were the last so far,” Ted said.

Corgi sat down. “If someone else comes, do I give it back?”

“You haven’t picked it up.”

“Good. Then I’ve already given it back.”

He left the parcel where it was and nudged his ball over to Ted.

They rolled the ball towards the table. It stopped by the extra cup.

“Maybe ‘there’ means here,” said Corgi. “Whoever gets their cocoa last.”

Panda-Cake set the jug down. “That’ll be me if I have to pour it for everyone first.”

His own cup stood empty next to the jug.

Ted turned to the first clean page of his notebook.

He wrote DOOR on one line and COCOA on another.

“Presents?” said Corgi.

“We’ve all opened ours.”

“I know. But what if someone hasn’t?”

Ted wrote PRESENTS underneath. Now there were three things that “there” could mean.

Corgi went back to the tree. He held one end of the blue cord up in the light.

“Look at that knot,” he said. “The end goes back through twice.”

He pointed towards the wall. The library’s noticeboard hung from a cord with the very same knot.

Ted climbed onto a low stool so he could see. Both cords had three thin white strands twisted through the blue.

“Hooten keeps a whole spool of it in his drawer,” he said.

Just then, Hooten opened that drawer. Inside, beside the string, lay a little silver camera.

Before Ted could ask about the cord, there was a knock.

Corgi rushed over. Hooten reached the door first.

On the step stood a young hare in a plum coat. Her ears stuck out of a knitted hood. She held a tin against her chest.

“I’m Moss,” said the hare. “We moved into the house by the bridge. The snow was up to my knees.”

She looked at the folded wrapping paper.

“I’ve missed it, haven’t I?”

“The cocoa’s warm,” said Panda-Cake. “Come and show me what’s in your tin.”

Moss had brought ginger biscuits. Some were shaped like hares. One was shaped like half a hare.

“I dropped that one,” she said.

“That’s the one I’d choose,” said Corgi. “It’s already started.”

Moss smiled and took off her coat. Her ears sprang straight out of the hood.

Hooten poured cocoa into the extra cup. Ted fetched a chair so Moss could sit at the table.

“You kept her cup ready,” Ted said to Hooten.

“I kept a cup ready,” said Hooten. “I didn’t know whose it would be.”

Ted thought about the box under the tree.

Ted held up his notebook.

“We guessed it might mean the door. Or the cocoa. Then Corgi said the presents. Is that what ‘there’ means?”

Hooten nodded. “I tied that parcel for whoever came after the others had opened theirs.”

“So there’d still be one,” said Corgi.

Ted picked up the box. “Moss, I think it’s yours.”

She tucked one long ear behind her shoulder so it wouldn’t dip in her cocoa. Then she pulled the loose end of the cord.

Inside the box lay a small wooden frame. There was no picture in it.

A folded note sat behind the glass. Moss read it aloud.

“Choose our first Christmas morning picture.”

Professor Hooten brought over the silver camera. “I thought we could put up a new one every Christmas,” he said. “You get to choose what goes in the first frame.”

“I can take a good one,” said Moss. “I take pictures of the birds by our bridge.”

She lifted the camera. Through it she could see a bit of the tree and most of Ted. Panda-Cake was hidden behind a chair.

“We’ll have to move the chairs.”

Moss put the chairs near the tree. She asked Hooten to sit down and Panda-Cake to stand behind him.

Ted sat on the floor. Corgi lay beside Ted with his nose on the red ball.

Moss raised the camera again. There was exactly one empty chair in the picture.

“That one’s for you,” said Ted.

“I’m usually behind the camera,” Moss said.

Hooten showed her a little switch. “This gives you ten seconds to get to the chair.”

Moss set the camera on a low wooden stool and aimed it at the tree. “I can get there in four.”

Moss pressed the button and hurried over. One, two, three, four. She made it.

Then Corgi tried to grin without letting go of his ball. It slipped from under his nose and bumped the stool.

Click.

“I think it took me jumping,” said Corgi.

Hooten held out the camera. On the little screen was a crooked picture. The tree leaned sideways. Corgi was halfway out of the picture, with his tail straight up.

Everyone else was laughing. Moss was right in the middle of them.

“We could take another,” said Hooten.

“I choose that one,” said Moss.

She put the empty frame on the shelf next to the tree. Ted opened his notebook and wrote the date, ready for when they printed the picture.

Corgi carried his ball to the door. He waited there until everybody else had gone through.

books.title: Sub-Zero and the Great Snowball Truce

pages.text:
The morning after Christmas, snow covered the whole hill.

Sub-Zero slid down on his tummy. At the bottom he slid a bit farther, just because he could.

“Still going!” he called.

Biscuit-Bouncer scooped up a soft snowball. He threw it at the stump.

Poff!

A little white cloud rose from the bark.

Two Baby Bulldogs bounced out of the snow. “Let’s play!”

They made two teams. Sub-Zero and the brindle Bulldog wore blue mittens. Biscuit and the fawn Bulldog wore red.

Hop-Tart climbed onto a flat stone. His yellow hat was easy to spot.

“I’ll keep score.”

Hop-Tart waved a white flag.

“Throw at coats, low and soft. When I lift the flag, everybody stops.”

Biscuit rolled his first snowball. Sub-Zero packed his just tight enough to pick up.

“Ready?” called Hop.

Four mittens went down.

“Go!”

Four soft snowballs went up.

One landed on a stump. One went nowhere much at all.

Biscuit’s snowball caught the blue Bulldog on the hem of his coat.

“One to red!” called Hop.

Then Sub-Zero slid past Biscuit. Biscuit spun to see where he’d gone.

Poff! Snow caught the back of Biscuit’s coat.

“That was very quick,” said Biscuit. He shook out his coat.

“Can I have a spot where I can stop?”

“Of course,” said Hop. He pushed a yellow flag into the snow. “Rest beside this one.”

The fawn Bulldog wanted a spot to roll snowballs. Hop put up a red flag.

Sub-Zero asked for a clear bit of slope to slide down. Hop put up two blue flags.

“Easy,” said Hop.

Then the blue Bulldog asked where all the good snow was.

“By the little drift,” said Hop. He put a green flag there.

“What about the big drift?”

Hop had one green flag left.

Biscuit rolled a snowball by the yellow flag.

“Red is for rolling!” called the fawn Bulldog.

Sub-Zero slid between the greens.

“Did green mean go?” he called.

Hop opened his mouth. Then he closed it.

“Stop,” called Hop, and raised the white flag. He took off his yellow hat to shake out the snow.

He hooked the brim over a peg on the low fence post. The hat hung open side up.

The whole field stopped.

“Would you like a bigger rest spot?” Hop asked Biscuit.

Biscuit looked at the flags. “I like throwing,” he said. “I don’t like turning round and finding snow on my back.”

Sub-Zero sat down beside him.

“I mostly like sliding,” said Sub-Zero.

The blue Bulldog thought about that.

“I like rolling a great big snowball.”

“I like knocking things over,” said the fawn Bulldog.

Hop looked towards the fence.

Three empty tubs stood under the fence rail.

“We could throw at those,” said Biscuit.

He tipped one over with a soft snowball.

Sub-Zero slid over and set it up again. “I could do that all day.”

They set all three tubs on their rims in a row. They pulled up the little flags.

Hop kept just his white flag.

“Throw on my ‘Go’. When the snow lands, I lift the flag. Then the sliders can go.”

“Do we still need teams?” asked the brindle Bulldog.

“We can wear our mittens,” said Biscuit.

“Let’s see how many turns we can finish together,” said Hop.

He held up one paw to count.

“Ready? Go!”

Biscuit and the fawn Bulldog threw at the tubs.

Poff! Poff!

Two tubs tipped. The little one wobbled and stayed up.

Hop lifted the white flag. Everybody waited until the snow had landed.

“Sliders ready?”

Down went Sub-Zero and the blue Bulldog.

Up went the tubs.

Sub-Zero slid past the last one, scooted back on his bottom and gave it a little pat.

“Still going,” he said.

The Bulldogs swapped places. Hop played a turn, too. His first snowball rolled along the ground and stopped just short.

The fawn Bulldog set her paws on a tub anyway.

“I’m practising,” she said.

“One last go,” said Hop.

Biscuit picked up a snowball as soft as a bun. Hop dropped the flag.

Biscuit threw. The little tub tipped. The snowball bounced off its rim and went up towards the fence.

Plip.

The snowball dropped straight into Hop’s hat.

Everyone looked at the hat. It hung a little lower than it had before.

Hop looked down at his flag. “I didn’t make a rule for that.”

Sub-Zero slid over to the fence and took down the hat.

“One point to yellow,” he said.

“I win?” asked Hop.

“The hat wins,” said Biscuit. He tipped the snowball into the empty little tub.

They went to the bench for cocoa. Hop turned his hat right way up and put it on.

A single bit of snow slid down his ear.

“Can the hat have another go tomorrow?” Biscuit asked.

Hop tucked the hat under his arm.

“The hat is resting.”

Below the bench, three tubs waited in a row. In the smallest one sat a snowball, shaped almost exactly like a yellow hat.

books.title: Captain Beakon and the Bell Across the Bay

pages.text:
Polly Roger could hear the ferry before she could see its lights. The engine slowed outside the harbour wall and the loose handle on the cabin door began to chatter. She made the same sound with her beak. A passenger reached behind her to steady the handle, then gave her a look.

“I might need that noise,” Polly said.

Captain Beakon strapped his brass telescope into its case. “You collect noises the way other people collect shells.”

“Shells take up room,” said Polly. Then the ferry turned and the harbour came into view.

The town curved round the head of the bay. On the west side, a wide stone quay ran out below the bell tower. The market stood at the head, where two streets met. From there a narrow path followed the east shore past the old net shed and ended at a blue boathouse.

Belgian-Waffle was waiting at the landing with his messenger bag strapped over his waffle vest. He took them to the market wall, where he said the harbour bell sounded best.

Polly could see both shores from there if she stood on tiptoe.

They'd come to join the Christmas lantern procession. Last December, Beakon had promised to bring Polly back for the bell. Tonight was the rehearsal. At the real procession in two evenings, the tower would ring, the first lantern would light at the market, and everyone would walk east to the blue boathouse.

“People can hear it behind closed windows,” said Belgian. “No one has to stand in the cold just to know when we're leaving.”

He tapped the tune on his bag. Two close taps. A space long enough to take a breath. One on its own.

Marnie, the badger who ran the market, handed Polly a bundle of paper lanterns to unfold. Marnie could lift a long trestle table by herself, but asked for help with anything that creased.

“Leave the gaps between the stalls clear,” she told Belgian. “When the bell goes, the whole quay comes through at once.”

On the west side, a tall brown rook crossed the quay in a grey coat. Belgian pointed him out. Rowe looked after the bell and had rung it every December for twenty-three years.

Every clock on the market wall said a slightly different time. Marnie watched Rowe instead. He raised one wing beside the tower door and went inside. From across the bay, the laundrette windows shone behind him.

The first two strokes came so close that the low note of the first was still humming under the second. Polly knew exactly how long to wait. She held her breath and squeezed a fold flat in the paper lantern.

The third stroke didn't come.

She looked up. Rowe had lowered his wing. She could no longer see the tower door.

Marnie called towards the west quay. A figure in grey came out of the tower and lifted both wings: stop.

“Keep the paper dry,” Marnie said. Someone had started to light a practice lantern and she went to speak to them.

For a few seconds Polly thought the bell itself had fallen. Then she realised how many sounds that would have made.

Beakon didn't move from the wall. “What did you hear?”

“Two strokes,” said Polly. “The second one went flat sooner than I expected.”

“Tell me that again later,” he said.

In the café, Belgian laid a dry napkin over each of their damp lanterns. He liked putting things in order when he couldn't fix them. Marnie came in and told the room that Rowe had set the rope aside until the bell could be checked. The procession was still on.

A few people began telling stories about the time snow shut the market or the time the power went out. In all of their stories, somebody rang the bell anyway.

Belgian stacked the napkins too neatly. Polly didn't ask what he was thinking.

Next afternoon, Polly helped Beakon carry a box of lantern hooks to the east path. The boards of the old net shed had been bleached grey. Beyond it, the blue boathouse sat with its long side to the water. No boat had been kept there since the slipway wore out. Now somebody had planted winter herbs in pots along the dry side.

“Ada Reed looks after it,” said Belgian. “She lets people mend nets there if it rains.”

One of the pots was wedging the side door open. Polly smelled damp rope and rosemary.

Belgian made two trips to the market while they fastened the hooks. On his third, he brought a long wooden box on a handcart. One board at the end rattled with every bump.

Polly offered to take a handle. Belgian shook his head.

“Easy from here. I've got to get it to the bend before dark.”

He took the east path past the net shed. Polly turned back to hold the ladder from ground level while Beakon secured the last lantern hook. When she looked again, Belgian and the box were out of sight.

Polly had hardly got her claws warm when Marnie asked whether she could hear the bell from anywhere but the market wall. Polly began listing places. Then she saw what Marnie actually wanted.

“I can tell people if I hear it,” Polly said.

“You could wait at the wall,” Marnie said. “Some of the stallholders think we're calling the whole thing off. I could use somebody who listens.”

Polly stood a little straighter. She was used to being asked to repeat what she'd heard. This was the first time anybody had asked her to be responsible for it.

Near dusk, the market fell quiet for the time it took the ferry to pass the harbour wall. Polly leaned over the rail.

Two strokes. A gap. Then one on its own.

She knew the tune before she had time to decide where it came from. She turned towards the tower. The low window was dark. A moment later she caught a little knock from the east, where the blue boathouse should be.

“It's back,” said a man beside her.

Polly stared out at the bay. “I don't think it's back in the same place.”

In the café, Polly tried the two sounds for Beakon. For the first night, she lowered her note and let it out slowly. For the second night, she cut the note off sooner and added the little knock with her beak against the side of her cup.

“The tune is the same,” she said.

“And the sound?”

“The notes were higher. Shorter, too. I didn't notice until I tried it.”

Beakon stirred his tea. “Someone rehearsing on another bell would do it.”

Polly had already got a picture of the big bell on a cart. It was hard to put down.

The ferry pilot came in carrying an empty flask. She'd been out on the water when the bell rang and was sure it had come from the west.

“I was facing the west,” she said.

“Were you outside?” asked Polly.

“My window was shut. I opened it after the second stroke.”

She traced the shore in the air with a finger. The ferry had been turning. By the last stroke, she had been facing the market again.

“I still think west,” she said. “But I couldn't swear to it.”

At the far end of the café, a fox called Len told someone he'd seen a crate on the east path. He kept repeating how wide it was. Polly sat beside him and asked if the crate had been on a handcart.

“The cart rattled,” said Len. “I heard it after the bell.”

“I saw it in the afternoon.”

Len rubbed the window with his sleeve. “Could have been. I've been moving wet chairs off this path all day. After a while everything with wheels sounds like the same chair.”

Polly drew the three things she knew on the back of a market leaflet. The tower on the west. The tune on the east. The cart that had gone round the head of the bay.

She put a question mark on the cart. Then she made the question mark smaller, as if that might make the rest of the drawing more useful.

Belgian saw it when he passed their table.

“Is that my cart?”

“It's a cart,” said Polly.

He waited. She folded the paper so the drawing was inside.

By morning, somebody at the market was saying the bell had been moved without permission. Somebody else said it had been sold. Nobody could say who had first told them.

Polly went down to the tower with Beakon. A wooden board blocked the entrance, with a fresh notice to say the bell would stay silent while a bell specialist looked at it. Above them, the square louvred opening was too far away to tell what was behind it.

Beakon sat on the seawall. “We can wait for Rowe.”

Polly had hoped they could do something quicker.

Rowe was at the quay hatch signing out a set of life rings for the procession. He recognised Beakon and came over.

“You stopped after the second stroke,” Polly said.

“Yes.”

“Did the bell go somewhere?”

“It's hanging where it did yesterday,” he said. “And where it did the day before that.”

He didn't seem offended. He looked tired. When Polly asked if they could see, Rowe showed her a photograph he had taken that morning for the specialist. The bell hung in its frame, a sea-grey cone with a nicked rim.

Rowe enlarged the picture until a dark line showed near the rim. From the ground, Polly would have missed it.

“I heard a change on the second stroke,” he said. “I stopped. We'll leave the rope tied back until we know more.”

Beakon asked what it would take to move the bell.

“A crew, a lift and room on the west quay. You can't get it through the stair door on a handcart.” Rowe slid the screen shut. “Wish you could. The specialist wouldn't have to bring so much gear.”

On the way back, Belgian was stacking empty crates beside the lane. At his feet lay the same long box, upside down and empty. A delivery slip stuck up beneath its lid.

“You can look,” he said. “Don't get it wet. It's my copy.”

Polly read the familiar words at the top and the short description underneath. Wooden stand. East shore. Ada Reed.

“Did she say what it was for?”

“No. I carried a stand with two folding legs. It came out at the boathouse. Then I brought the box back.”

As they walked, Polly tried to fit what Belgian had said to the tune she’d heard. A wooden stand might be part of another bell. It could also be a place to hang nets or dry lanterns.

“What did you think it was for?” she asked.

Belgian lifted his good wing. “I thought it was a stand.”

She took that for a joke until she saw his face. He'd been answering her honestly the whole time and was beginning to wonder what answer she wanted.

“It helps,” she said. “I should have said that first.”

The market wall was dry again. Polly stood on her usual stone and did the tune in her head.

If the first night had happened at the tower, its note had reached her over open water. On the second night, the last short note had arrived at the same time as a shutter or latch knocked on the east shore. She remembered the boathouse door being held open with a pot. She remembered the smell of rosemary.

She had a place, a sound and a delivery. What she needed was a way to see whether they belonged together.

Marnie found her at the wall and handed her a piece of chalk. On the board by the market gate was a question that someone had written in a hurry. Where will the bell ring?

“I was going to write that there might be a drum,” said Marnie. “But people see guesses and turn them into plans.”

“I heard it from the east,” said Polly.

“You heard a sound. If you write where, someone will ask who.”

Polly looked down at the chalk. She thought of Belgian saying he'd carried a stand.

Polly drew an arrow towards the east track. Ask Belgian where the bell went, she wrote underneath. If he'd carried something for a rehearsal, he must know the town would want to hear it again. She imagined him saying so at the market wall, where people knew to trust his directions.

Marnie had moved to help a stallholder with a table. There was time to rub the words out and write something smaller.

Someone behind Polly read the board aloud. Another voice said, “So that's what was in the box.”

Belgian was outside the market gate trying to get his handcart through a knot of people. Len stopped beside it.

“Where'd you take the bell?” he asked.

“What bell?”

Len pointed at the board. Belgian looked up just as Polly reached it. She wiped the writing away with her sleeve. Wet chalk made a broad white bruise on the slate.

“It never went anywhere,” she said.

Len took his hand off the cart. Someone at the back said that was easy to say now. Belgian wheeled the cart into the lane.

Polly caught up at the net shed. “I was trying to tell people you knew what had happened.”

“Then why didn't you ask me if I knew?”

Polly could only think of things that would make it worse. She waited while Belgian pulled the cart under the eaves and wedged a stone against one wheel.

“Some people count on me to carry things without making it everybody else's business,” he said. “I told you what was on the slip because I thought it would help.”

“It did,” Polly said. He looked at her then.

Beakon was on the seawall, looking through his telescope at the gulls. He lowered it as Polly came to sit beside him.

“I knew the bell was still in the tower,” she said. “I thought if I wrote it that way, people would ask Belgian about the other one.”

“You wrote the riddle as though you already knew the answer.”

“Can you tell them what I meant?”

“I can go with you,” said Beakon.

They watched a gull try to land on a post, miss, and turn for another go.

Rowe was sitting outside the café with his flask, waiting for a call from the specialist. Polly asked whether she could say what he'd shown her in the photograph.

“You can say the bell is still in the tower,” he said. “And that it won't ring tonight.”

“Will people mind?”

“Some will. I mind.”

He took a swallow of tea. “I've had my hand on that rope every December for a very long time. Being the one who lets go is part of the job too.”

At the market board, Marnie gave Polly a clean rag and stood next to her while she wiped off the last white streak. Len was helping stack chairs close enough to hear.

Polly wrote three short lines. The tower bell is still in place. It will stay quiet until it has been checked. Belgian delivered a stand.

“Put your name underneath,” Marnie said.

That was the part Polly had wanted yesterday. She hadn't expected it to feel quite so different when the words were true.

Polly found Belgian untying a bundle of lantern hooks. She asked him to read the board if he wanted. Then she told him she'd been wrong to put his name on the first notice.

He took his time with a knot.

“All right,” he said. “But if you want to ask Ada about the stand, you ask her. I can show you the path.”

He undid the knot and shook out the cord, which was still tangled in the middle. He gave Polly one end to hold.

They walked east with Beakon. From the narrow path, Polly could see the broad west quay and the level place where a crane might stand beside the tower. Nothing on this side was wide enough for that. A handcart could go east carrying a wooden stand. A great bell could stay exactly where it was.

At the net shed, a loose board knocked in the wind. Polly stopped.

It was the sort of sound she'd heard after the third stroke. The two sounds had overlapped. They didn't have to come from the same thing.

At the boathouse the pot of rosemary sat a little way from the side door. One leaf had been trapped in the gap. Belgian stayed by the path while Polly knocked.

An otter in a rolled-up rust jumper opened the door. The wet weather had curled the fine fur round her ears.

“I'm Ada,” she said. “If you're here about the lantern brackets, they're ready.”

“I'm here because I heard the tune,” said Polly. “And because I said something at the market before I knew what it meant.”

Ada studied Polly for long enough that she heard the water hiss against the old slipway. Then Ada opened the door a little wider. A worktable, a coil of net and several shallow trays of screws filled the dry part of the room. A small brass bell hung from a folding wooden stand beside the far window.

It was about as wide as a dinner plate. For a moment Polly felt foolish for imagining the tower bell in a crate.

“Does it sound how I think?” she asked.

“That depends what you heard.”

Ada took a small handled striker from a felt pouch. She asked Beakon to hold the door during the demonstration.

Two bright strokes close together. A breath. One bright stroke on its own.

Polly knew the tune. She waited until the last note had faded, then made the short, high sound she'd kept in her head. In the doorway Belgian looked up.

“That's what we heard,” said Beakon.

“Almost,” said Polly. While Ada put the striker away, Beakon let the heavy door swing gently towards the catch.

Knock.

“The pot slipped yesterday,” Ada said. She picked up the trapped leaf and brushed it off the sill. “The door swung in as I finished the tune.”

Polly made the knock once, softly. Then she told Ada about the dark tower, the pilot turning in her boat, and Len remembering the wheels later than he'd heard them. She could make a story with every bit now. She didn't need the cart to carry anything except what it had carried.

Belgian was looking at the bell. Ada asked if he'd like to see where the stand folded.

Ada used to teach the tune to new lantern carriers. The big bell was hard to get permission to ring, so she bought a little practice bell and used it indoors. Her partner Kit used to listen from the other shore and make a signal with a handkerchief when she got the gap right.

“We stopped practising out here after Kit died,” she said. “This winter I thought I could bear to do it again.”

She reached over and put one paw against the little brass skirt. It was already still.

“When Marnie said the big bell had gone quiet, I asked for the stand,” Ada said. “I thought I might have something to offer. Yesterday was a trial with the door open. I hadn't intended to announce anything.”

Polly thought of the chalk in her sleeve. A little brass bell could reach the market wall. There were flats up behind the tower, and houses beside the road. There would be people waiting for a note they could hear from their own tables.

“Would you ring it tonight if Marnie asked?” she said.

Ada looked across at the square opening in the tower.

“Someone will say I want to take Rowe's place.”

“He could tell them himself,” said Beakon.

Polly didn't know if he would or if he should have to. She asked Ada what she'd want the notice to say. Ada hung the little bell on a wall hook while she tested a wooden joint of the stand.

“I'd want it to say practice bell,” she said. “And I'd want people at the far flats to know that it won't sound as loud.”

They brought Marnie and Rowe to the boathouse by the east path. Ada showed them the stand before she showed them the bell. Rowe asked if he could try one stroke, and she handed him the felt pouch.

The high note surprised him. He laughed once and waited for it to fade. Then he and Ada worked out who would ring, who would light the first lantern, and where the lantern carrier should stand.

Polly watched them move the stand back from the door. This time somebody put the pot in a place where it couldn't slip.

Marnie had time to change the market notices before dusk. Rowe wrote his own line beneath hers about the inspection. Belgian walked copies down the west shore, all the way to the flats.

Polly went with him. One neighbour couldn't hear the high note from her sitting room. She could see the end of the quay, so they asked whether she'd like a lantern raised there in answer. She said yes, if it was above the rail and somebody could keep it still.

Belgian knew exactly which post she meant. At the market wall on the way back, he pointed across to it so Polly would know it too.

On the way back, Len called to them from the café door. He was trying to pick up too many folded chairs at once.

“I thought it was your cart,” he said to Belgian.

“It rattles most days,” Belgian said. “You can help me quiet the loose board after Christmas.”

Polly took the chair at the top of Len's pile. He hadn't asked for help. She waited a moment before taking another, and he moved his hand so she could get a better grip.

The market stalls glowed as the sky darkened. For the first time that week the wind dropped. Some people walked west to watch the tower. Marnie asked them to turn round so they could also see the boathouse.

Polly carried the first paper lantern down to the market wall. She had folded it on the rehearsal night. A small crease still ran down one side. She smoothed it with her claw, then left it there.

Across the water, the old tower kept its dark square window. Ada opened the blue door.

Polly heard the first bright stroke and then the second. She knew how long the empty space ought to last. Once, she would have filled it by copying the sound herself. Now she waited.

The third stroke reached the wall. On the west quay, the answering lantern rose above the rail and held there, as steady as a window.

Marnie brought her flame to Polly's lantern. It lit along the crease first. The crowd behind her began walking east in a slow line.

By the boathouse, Ada was passing out lantern hooks. The little bell was back in the shelter of the doorway. As Polly passed, Ada put her paw on the top of the stand.

“Next year we could have both,” she said. “The tower for the procession, and this one for practice while we're learning.”

Polly asked whether she could come when they tried it again.

“Bring Belgian,” Ada said. “He knows which board on this floor makes that noise.”

Belgian looked down. He took one step to the right. The board gave a small, familiar creak.

After the procession, Polly went back to the wall with Beakon. He asked if she was going to do the bell again for him.

“In a minute,” she said.

The ferry was nearly through the harbour opening. Across the water, the answering lantern was still there. Polly could just see Belgian holding it up for the neighbour at the window. One of his wings began to dip, then steadied.

Polly set her own lantern on the wall. While the light on the other shore stayed up, she listened to everything else.

books.title: Everybody Brought Potatoes

pages.text:
The leaves in Bark-B-Q’s garden had turned the colour of toast.

“This year,” said Bark-B-Q, “I’m having Friendsgiving. A Thanksgiving feast with all my friends, here, under the apple tree. Everyone brings one dish.”

He wagged so hard that three leaves fell off the tree.

Eggs-Benedict arrived the next morning with a clipboard and a sharp pencil.

“One dish each is a lovely idea,” she said. “But what if everybody brings soup?”

She drew a sign-up sheet with two columns, **Name** and **Dish**. Then she drew a timing chart, so every dish would be hot at exactly the right moment.

“Write yours first,” she said, “to show everyone how.”

Bark-B-Q took the pencil and wrote in big letters on the top line:

*Bark-B-Q — potatoes, roasted.*

“Perfect,” said Eggs-Benedict. “Now we need someone fast to take it round.”

Belgian-Waffle was the fastest messenger in the woods. He tucked the sign-up sheet under one wing and took off.

“Every door before lunch!” he called.

Over the duck pond, a gust of wind came out of nowhere. It snatched the sheet from under his wing.

The paper flipped twice, sailed over the reeds and landed in the water. By the time Belgian-Waffle fished it out, the ink had run into one long blue puddle.

Belgian-Waffle looked at the soggy paper. He thought about flying back to tell Eggs-Benedict.

Then he thought about her sharp pencil.

“I read the top line,” he told himself. “I know what it said. I’ll just tell everybody.”

Meow-inara opened her door. “Is it the sign-up sheet? What should I bring?”

“Potatoes,” said Belgian-Waffle. “I think.”

“Potatoes,” said Meow-inara. “All right.”

“Potatoes?” said Leo-Lemonade. “I always bring lemonade.”

“This year it’s potatoes,” said Belgian-Waffle. “I’m fairly sure.”

“Potatoes? Not bread?” said French-Toast.

“Definitely potatoes,” said Belgian-Waffle. He was getting better at saying it.

On Friendsgiving afternoon, the long table stood under the apple tree. Bark-B-Q had his potatoes ready for roasting. Eggs-Benedict pinned her timing chart to the tree trunk.

“Four o’clock, soup,” she read. “Quarter past, bread. Half past, lemonade. Quarter to five…”

The gate creaked. Meow-inara came in, pulling a sack.

It was full of potatoes.

“Lovely,” said Bark-B-Q, a little puzzled. “Two lots of potatoes. That’s fine.”

The gate creaked again. Leo-Lemonade came in, pushing a wheelbarrow.

In the wheelbarrow was one potato. It was the biggest potato anyone had ever seen.

“I wanted to bring a good one,” he said.

Then French-Toast arrived with a basket of long orange potatoes.

“Sweet potatoes,” he said proudly.

Everybody looked at Eggs-Benedict.

“A sweet potato isn’t a potato at all,” said Eggs-Benedict. “It grows on a completely different plant. It’s a cousin of the morning glory flower.”

“So I’m the only one who didn’t bring potatoes?” said French-Toast.

“You’re the only one who did it by accident,” said Leo-Lemonade.

Then the gate creaked one last time. Belgian-Waffle came in with a small bag of potatoes and a very small voice.

Everybody looked at Belgian-Waffle.

Belgian-Waffle looked at his feet.

“The sheet fell in the duck pond,” he said. “The only thing I could read was the top line. So I told everybody potatoes.”

For a moment, nobody said anything.

Bark-B-Q looked at the timing chart. Four o’clock, soup. There was no soup. Quarter past, bread. There was no bread. Half past, lemonade. There was one enormous potato in a wheelbarrow.

His tail stopped wagging. “Friendsgiving is ruined,” he said.

Eggs-Benedict took the timing chart down from the tree. She turned it over to the clean side.

“Then we need a new chart,” she said.

She wrote **POTATOES** in the middle of the paper and drew a circle round it. Then she drew lines coming out of the circle, like the spokes of a wheel.

“Who can make something out of potatoes?” she asked.

“Potato soup,” said Meow-inara.

“Potato bread,” said French-Toast. “And a sweet potato pie.”

“Potato waffles,” said Belgian-Waffle. “I make very good waffles.”

“Roast potatoes,” said Bark-B-Q, and his tail started to wag again, just a little.

Leo-Lemonade looked at his enormous potato. “I only know how to make lemonade.”

“Then you can help me,” said Eggs-Benedict, “and we’ll make the biggest pile of mashed potato in the woods.”

She cooked. He mashed. Leo-Lemonade turned out to be extremely good at mashing.

Soon every pot and pan in Bark-B-Q’s kitchen was busy. Meow-inara stirred the soup. French-Toast kneaded the dough. Belgian-Waffle heated the waffle iron.

Outside, Bark-B-Q turned the potatoes on the grill, slowly, the way a good roast likes.

Eggs-Benedict checked her new chart. There were no times on it at all. Just one line at the bottom: *Everything at five o’clock.*

At five o’clock exactly, everything was ready.

They carried it out to the table under the apple tree. Potato soup. Potato bread. Potato waffles. Roast potatoes. A mountain of mash. And a sweet potato pie.

“Six dishes,” said Eggs-Benedict, counting them with her pencil. “Six different ways.”

Bark-B-Q looked at the table for a long time.

“It isn’t what I planned,” he said.

“It’s better,” said Meow-inara. “Nobody in the whole woods has ever had a potato feast.”

Before they ate, everybody said one thing they were thankful for.

“Eggs-Benedict,” said Bark-B-Q, “for the second chart.”

“Leo-Lemonade,” said Eggs-Benedict, “for the mashing.”

“The duck pond,” said Leo-Lemonade, and everyone laughed, even Belgian-Waffle.

When it was Bark-B-Q’s turn again, he turned to Belgian-Waffle.

“And I’m thankful for you.”

“Me?” said Belgian-Waffle. “I ruined everything.”

“You made it the best Friendsgiving we’ve ever had,” said Bark-B-Q. “You just did it by accident.”

They ate until the lanterns came on in the apple tree. The sweet potato pie went last.

“The only thing on the table that wasn’t a potato,” said French-Toast, “and it was the first thing to go.”

As everybody was leaving, Eggs-Benedict took out a fresh sheet of paper. She wrote next year’s sign-up sheet there and then.

On the top line, in big letters, she wrote: *Everybody — potatoes.*

Underneath, in smaller letters, she wrote: *Belgian-Waffle — please carry this very carefully.*

books.title: Corgi-on-the-Cob and the Harvest Table

pages.text:
On Thanksgiving morning, there was frost on Corgi-on-the-Cob’s corn patch. The leaves had nearly all come down, and the stalks rustled in the cold.

Nutmeg’s invitation was pinned to his door. *Come to the harvest table in my barn. Bring one thing.*

“I’ll bring the corn,” said Corgi. “Obviously.”

He picked the fattest cobs he could find and laid them in his basket.

“One cob, two cobs, three cobs, four. Five cobs, six cobs.” He wagged. “Six cobs for six friends.”

Corgi took the basket handle in his mouth and set off. The basket was heavy. It swung left and right with every step.

The path went down to the stream. Five flat stones crossed it, one after another.

On the middle stone, the basket swung too far. Two cobs tipped out. Plop. Plop.

They bobbed away down the stream.

“Four cobs for six friends!” said Corgi. “That’s not right at all.”

Something round and green paddled out from under the bank. It was Shelly-Pop.

She nudged one cob back with her nose, then the other. “Corn floats,” she said. “Lucky for you.”

“Six cobs for six friends,” said Corgi, putting them back. “Thank you, Shelly-Pop!”

“I’m going to the barn too,” said Shelly-Pop. “I’ll walk with you. Slowly.”

After the stream came the hill. It was steep, and the fallen leaves made it slippery.

Corgi has very short legs. The basket bumped on every step. Shelly-Pop was slower still.

Clip, clop. Pita-Pan came trotting up behind them.

“Goats are good at hills,” he said. He took the basket handle in his teeth and climbed. Corgi pushed the basket from below to keep it level.

At the top of the hill, Corgi counted again.

“One, two, three, four, five.” He counted again, slower. “Five.”

One cob was missing.

They looked back down the hill. At the bottom, a huge pile of leaves was jumping all by itself.

Out popped Hop-Tart, with a cob in his paws.

“Is this anybody’s?” he called. “It was in my jumping pile.”

“Six cobs for six friends!” said Corgi. “Thank you, Hop-Tart.”

Now there were four of them walking along the lane to the barn: Corgi, Shelly-Pop, Pita-Pan and Hop-Tart. Corgi carried the basket the whole way, and he didn’t drop a single cob.

Nutmeg’s red barn was full of warm light. A long table stood in the middle, made of planks laid across hay bales. There were gourds down the middle and a jug of autumn leaves.

“The corn’s here!” called Nutmeg.

Ted-E-Bear had brought soup. Panda-Cake had brought rolls, still warm. Nutmeg had made an apple pie with a leaf cut in the top.

Panda-Cake cooked the corn in a big pot on the barn stove, then rolled each cob in butter.

Everyone sat down. Before anyone ate, Nutmeg stood up.

“This is a thank-you table,” she said. “Before we eat, everybody says one friend they’re thankful for.”

“Panda-Cake,” said Ted. “For the blanket fort.”

“Nutmeg,” said Panda-Cake. “For the barn.”

“Ted,” said Nutmeg. “For carrying the table with me, plank by plank.”

Then it was Corgi’s turn. He thought very hard.

“Shelly-Pop,” he said. “And Pita-Pan. And Hop-Tart.” He looked worried. “Is three allowed?”

“Thank-yous don’t run out,” said Nutmeg.

Panda-Cake set the steaming corn on the table, and Corgi handed it round.

“One for Nutmeg. One for Ted. One for Panda-Cake. One for Shelly-Pop. One for Pita-Pan. One for Hop-Tart.”

Six cobs for six friends.

Then Corgi looked down at his own plate. It was empty.

He counted the chairs. There were seven. He had counted six friends, and he had forgotten to count himself.

“That’s all right,” said Corgi. He made his ears stand up straight. “I had lots of corn this summer.”

Nobody said anything for a moment.

Then Hop-Tart snapped a piece off the end of his cob. Snap. He put it on Corgi’s plate.

Shelly-Pop did the same. Snap.

Then Pita-Pan. Then Ted. Then Panda-Cake. Then Nutmeg.

Snap, snap, snap, snap.

Corgi looked at his plate.

“Six pieces,” he said. “That’s more corn than anybody!”

“Six pieces from six friends,” said Nutmeg.

They ate the soup and the rolls and the buttery corn and nearly all the pie.

Outside, the frost came back. Inside, the barn stayed warm right up to the rafters.

When the stars came out, Corgi walked home with Shelly-Pop, Pita-Pan and Hop-Tart. He carried the empty basket.

“One friend, two friends, three friends,” he counted.

“And you,” said Hop-Tart.

“And me,” said Corgi. “I’m counting me this time.”

books.title: Ted-E-Bear and the Jar of Good Things

pages.text:
On the first day of the year, Ted-E-Bear found an empty honey jar at the back of his cupboard. He washed it, dried it and pushed a cork into the top.

Then he wrote a note on a scrap of paper, folded it twice and dropped it in.

“There,” he said. “One good thing.”

After that, whenever something good happened, Ted wrote it down. Some notes were on yellow paper, some on blue and some on the backs of old shopping lists.

He never read them again. He just watched the jar fill up, a little at a time, like snow on a windowsill.

Now it was the last day of the year. The jar was so full that the cork squeaked when Ted pushed it in.

Professor Hooten was having a New Year’s Eve party at the library, and Ted had a plan. He tied a red ribbon round the jar’s neck.

“I’m going to read the whole year out loud,” he told Corgi-on-the-Cob. “From the very first note to the very last.”

Corgi trotted beside him all the way to the library, which was unusual. Corgi usually ran ahead.

“What if it’s boring?” said Ted. “A whole year is a lot of things.”

“It won’t be boring,” said Corgi. He sounded very sure about it.

The library had a separate stone step in front of the door. Tonight it wore a thin, shiny coat of ice.

Ted’s paws were cold. The jar was heavy. He stepped up, and his boot slid one way while the jar slid the other.

The jar landed in a soft bank of snow and didn’t break. But the cork popped out, and the notes flew everywhere, like a flock of small paper birds.

Some landed on the step. Some landed in the snow. One blew all the way to the gate before Corgi caught it in his mouth.

Nutmeg and Panda-Cake came running out to help. They gathered every note they could find and carried them inside in a mixing bowl.

Ted looked into the bowl. His whole year was in there, all jumbled up.

“I never wrote the dates,” he said quietly. “Now I can’t read them in order.”

“Then we’ll put them back in order,” said Professor Hooten. “We’ll be detectives. Every note will have a clue.”

He fetched a long piece of string and tied it between two bookcases. Then he gave Panda-Cake a box of wooden pegs.

Nutmeg cut out twelve paper squares and wrote a month on each one: January, February, March, all the way to December. Panda-Cake pegged them along the string, one month after another.

“Now,” said Hooten. “Read us a note, Ted. Then tell us where it goes.”

Ted unfolded the first one. It was slightly damp.

> *Corgi and I built a snow bear. It looked more like a loaf.*

“Snow,” said Nutmeg. “So it’s winter. That could be January or February.”

“Or December,” said Panda-Cake.

“It was the very first note in the jar,” said Ted slowly. “I remember the loaf.” He pegged it under January.

The next note was on blue paper.

> *It rained on our picnic, so we had a puddle party instead. A duckling came.*

“Ducklings hatch in spring,” said Nutmeg. “April, maybe. Or May.”

Ted pegged it under April. Then he moved it to May. Then he moved it back to April, because that was when the big puddles were.

> *I read the whole welcome card out loud at the picnic. Corgi helped me with the first sounds.*

“That was the summer picnic on the cliff,” said Panda-Cake. “The day it was so hot the jam melted.”

Ted pegged it under July. He was beginning to enjoy this.

> *Eight lanterns. Two dark paths. Everyone got home.*

“The lantern walk,” said Hooten. “It gets dark early in autumn. That was October.”

> *Found the missing button. It was under the bench all along.*

Nobody could remember when that one happened. Not even Ted. They pegged it in the middle of the year and decided that was good enough.

There were three December notes: a shadow show, a snowball truce and a parcel under the tree on Christmas morning.

“December is getting crowded,” said Nutmeg.

“December is always crowded,” said Hooten.

Ted picked up the next note. The writing was big and wobbly, and at the bottom there was a sandy paw print.

> *At the sledging hill, Ted pulled my sled back up every time. Even when his legs were tired.*

Ted frowned. “I didn’t write this one.”

He unfolded another. Same wobbly writing. Same paw print.

> *Ted carried the last parcel all the way across the hall to Moss, who had only just moved here.*

And another.

> *It rained all afternoon, so Ted made his blanket fort big enough for Panda-Cake too. Even though it was only a small blanket.*

Ted sorted the bowl into two piles. His own neat notes went on one side. The wobbly notes went on the other.

The wobbly pile was nearly as big as his.

“These aren’t things that happened to me,” said Ted. “They’re things I did.”

Everyone turned to look at Corgi.

Corgi looked at the ceiling. Then at the floor. Then at the ceiling again.

“You left the jar on the shelf by your door,” he said at last. “And the cork isn’t very tight.”

“You put these in?” asked Ted. “All year?”

“Only when you weren’t looking,” said Corgi. “You only wrote the good things that happened to you. Nobody was writing down the good things you did.”

Ted didn’t say anything for a moment. He held the wobbly note about the sledging hill very carefully, as if it might fly away again.

“Where do Corgi’s notes go?” asked Panda-Cake.

That part was easy. Sledging meant snow, so that was winter. The last parcel was Christmas morning. The rainy blanket fort was spring.

Soon the string was full, from January to December. Blue notes, yellow notes and wobbly notes with paw prints, all mixed together.

Ted stepped back and looked at it.

It was a much longer year than he remembered. And there was much more of him in it.

Across the room, Professor Hooten’s wall of clocks showed eight o’clock. In one far-away city, it was midnight already.

Cluck O’Clock and Coop-Accino banged their pot lids. “Not yet, not yet… NOW!” everybody shouted. “Happy New Year, Dubai!”

“Now it’s your turn, Ted,” said Hooten.

So Ted read the year out loud, one note at a time, from January all the way to December.

When he read a neat note, everyone smiled. When he read a wobbly one, everyone looked at Corgi, and Corgi looked at the ceiling.

It wasn’t boring at all.

At the end, Ted took the notes off the string and put every one of them back in the honey jar. This time he pushed the cork in tightly.

Then he looked at the empty string.

“Next year needs a jar too,” he said. “A jar each.”

Hooten found four more jars in the library kitchen. One for Nutmeg. One for Panda-Cake. One for himself. And one for Corgi.

Nutmeg tied a ribbon round each one, and Panda-Cake wrote their names on the lids.

Ted tore a scrap of paper from his yellow notebook. He wrote something on it, folded it twice and dropped it into Corgi’s empty jar.

“What does it say?” asked Corgi.

“You’ll find out next New Year’s Eve,” said Ted.

It was the first good thing of the year. And it wasn’t even nine o’clock.

books.title: Cluck O’Clock and the Midnight That Came Early

pages.text:
On the last morning of the year, the twins built a snowman. Then Cluck O’Clock came in and wound his brass pocket watch. Click, click, click.

“Tonight I’m staying up for midnight,” he said. “The real one.”

“You fell asleep on Christmas Eve,” said Coop-Accino.

“After the sleigh,” said Cluck. “That’s different.”

Hen-Berry folded two paper hats at the kitchen table. A gold one for Cluck. A green one for Coop.

“Midnight is very late for a chicken,” she said.

“Midnight is when the new year starts,” said Cluck. “I want to be there when it does.”

That evening, they walked to the library in their hats. Lanterns hung along the path, and the snow squeaked under their feet.

Professor Hooten’s party was for families. It started at six o’clock and finished at nine.

“Nine isn’t midnight,” said Cluck.

“No,” said Hen-Berry. “It isn’t.”

Inside, Hooten had hung five round clocks in a row on the wall. Each clock had a little card underneath.

“Every clock keeps the time somewhere else,” said Hooten. “Some places start their day before we do, so their midnight comes sooner.”

He tapped the first clock. Its card said **Here**. Its hands said six o’clock.

Then he tapped the last clock. Its card said **Kiritimati**. Its hands said eight o’clock in the morning.

“That island is far out in the Pacific Ocean,” said Hooten. “Its midnight came while you were building your snowman.”

Coop stared. “It’s next year already? Somewhere?”

Cluck held his watch up next to the **Here** clock. Both said six.

“So whose midnight comes next?” he asked.

Hooten pointed to a clock with a card that said **Dubai**. “In two hours.”

There was cocoa and a long table of little cakes. By the door stood a basket of old pot lids and wooden spoons.

“For the countdowns,” said Hen-Berry, and gave one of each to the twins.

“Here’s my plan,” said Cluck. “We count down every midnight, all the way round, until we get to ours.”

Coop counted the clocks on her wingtips. “That’s a lot of midnights.”

“That’s the good bit,” said Cluck.

At eight o’clock, the hands of the Dubai clock crept up towards twelve. Everybody gathered under the wall.

“Ten, nine, eight…” counted Hooten.

“Not yet,” whispered Cluck, watching his watch. “Not yet…”

“…three, two, one…”

“NOW!”

Clang went the pot lids. Bang went the spoons. “Happy New Year, Dubai!” everyone shouted.

Cluck’s gold hat slid down over one eye. He didn’t mind at all.

Cluck ate one more cake, then half of another. Then he yawned. He hid the yawn behind his hat.

Coop saw. She didn’t say anything. She just moved the cake plate a little closer to him.

At nine o’clock, it was midnight in Nairobi. Everyone counted again.

“…three, two, one…”

“NOW!” shouted Coop.

“Now,” said Cluck, a moment later. He had been blinking at the wrong moment.

“Home time,” said Hen-Berry.

“But Cairo is next!” said Cluck. “It’s on the wall!”

Hooten bent down. “You have a clock of your own,” he said, nodding at the watch. “When it says ten o’clock, it will be midnight in Cairo.”

Hen-Berry pulled the twins’ little sled home along the lantern path. Coop walked beside it. Cluck rode, holding his watch up to the moon so he could see the hands.

“Nine twenty,” he reported. “Still awake.”

In bed, the twins kept their hats on. Cluck held the watch in his wing.

“Two minutes to Cairo,” he whispered.

“Wake me for it,” said Coop, and closed her eyes.

Tick. Tick. Tick. The watch sounded much louder in the dark.

Nine fifty-nine. Cluck’s eyes closed. They opened again. They closed again, a little longer.

The long hand reached twelve.

“Ten,” whispered Cluck. “Nine… eight… seven…”

Each number was slower than the one before.

“Four… three…”

Then nothing.

Coop opened one eye. Cluck was fast asleep, with the watch still in his wing.

“Two,” she whispered. “One. Now.”

She waved her wingtip like a very small flag. “Happy New Year, Cairo.”

Coop slipped the watch out of Cluck’s wing. She laid it on the table between their beds and tucked the chain under it so it couldn’t clink.

Then she lay down, too.

Much later, something went pop, far away. Then fizz.

Coop woke up. Over the trees, a little flower of gold light opened in the sky. Then a red one.

It was midnight here. The real one.

“Cluck,” whispered Coop. “Cluck! It’s ours!”

Cluck turned over. “Not yet,” he mumbled. “Not yet…”

And he went on sleeping.

His gold hat had fallen on the floor. Coop picked it up and set it gently back on his head.

“Now,” she whispered.

She watched the last spark fade over the trees, and went back to sleep.

In the morning, Cluck woke up with his hat on. It was crumpled on one side.

“Did I miss it?” he asked. “Did I miss our midnight?”

“You were there,” said Coop. “Hat and everything.”

Cluck picked up his watch. Seven o’clock on the first morning of the year.

“Then I’m awake for the very first morning,” he said. “All of it.”

He climbed to the window.

“Not yet,” he said. “Not yet…”

“NOW!” said Coop. And Cluck pulled back the curtain on a whole new year of snow.

books.title: Bark-B-Q and the Long Christmas Table

pages.text:
On Christmas morning, Bark-B-Q could see the sea between the posts of the picnic shelter. Sunlight danced on the bay, and a breeze stirred the paper stars he had hung along the shelter roof.

He carried a stack of plates down the sandy path to the long wooden table. A stripe of shade lay right across it. He could already picture everyone sitting there.

Bark-B-Q had made seven place cards. He had drawn a lemon for Leo-Lemonade and a tiny watch for Cluck O’Clock. His own card had a little star.

It went at the head of the table, in front of his blue chair. From there he could see every plate. If somebody needed more bread, he could be up in a second.

He clipped a timetable to his board. Drinks at eleven fifty-five. Lunch at twelve. Something sweet at twelve thirty.

Then he tucked a pencil behind his ear and walked all the way round the table. Two long benches, one blue chair and seven places. He tapped the back of his chair.

“I’ll see you at twelve,” he told it.

At the cooking station, away from the path and the tables, Bark-B-Q checked his lunch supplies. He covered the bread, then set out an empty jug and seven cups.

When he came back, the shade had slipped from the plates to one of the benches. He slid his card a little towards it.

Leo-Lemonade came up the path carrying a blue crate. Something clinked inside.

“My family puts lemon peel in the jug first,” he said. “Then the ice. If you put the ice in first, it’s very hard to give the lemon peel a proper stir.”

Bark-B-Q checked the timetable. Leo was seven minutes early.

Eggs-Benedict looked over his shoulder. She wore her gold crown, as usual. Today she had tucked a pencil beside one of its butter-yellow points.

“The drinks can wait in the cooler,” she said. “Shall I write that down?”

“There’s room right here,” Bark-B-Q said, and found a space between two very straight lines.

Panda-Cake arrived with a round tin hugged against her chest. Through the gap under the lid came the smell of orange.

“My aunt taught me to put little bits of candied peel on top,” she said. “One piece per slice. The first time I made it, I missed a slice and had to eat it myself.”

Bark-B-Q weighted the cloth with a stack of plates. He had just smoothed the other end when a warm gust set a napkin flapping against his paw.

Leo held down the bread basket. Panda caught the corner of the cloth.

“Thank you,” said Bark-B-Q. “A bit of breeze is nice.”

His blue chair was now in full sun.

Hen-Berry came through the gate with a dish covered by a red checked cloth. Cluck O’Clock and Coop-Accino each carried a small spoon in a clean teatowel.

“Cucumber salad,” said Coop, “with mint from our pot.”

“Use both spoons,” said Cluck. “I tried using one and a slice of cucumber landed on my foot.”

Coop tried a place on the bench. To reach her cup she had to lean forward until her feet lifted off the ground. When she sat back again, the cup was just where she had left it.

“I could move the cup,” she said. “But then I’d still have to reach the salad.”

Hen-Berry tried the other bench. The rail underneath left very little room to turn her feet.

“I’d do better with a chair I can pull out,” she said. “Is there one spare?”

Bark-B-Q looked at his blue chair. He could give her that one and stand by the bread basket. He was already reaching for it when Cluck spoke.

“Look at the shade,” said Cluck.

The shade that had stretched across the table that morning was now a dark wedge on the ground beside it. Cluck’s card, with its little watch, lay in the middle of the hot tabletop.

A warm gust ruffled the feathers behind his comb. The napkin flapped over the edge of the table. This time nobody had a free hand to catch it.

Bark-B-Q tucked the napkin under a plate. If he could move a bench closer to the shade, some of the trouble might go away.

He and Leo lifted one end and shuffled it sideways. They lowered the bench and stood back.

Cluck sat down. His feet were cool, but his plate was still in the sun. He tried to reach it without getting up.

“I think we’ve invented a bench for feet,” he said.

“Can we move the table as well?” Coop asked.

Bark-B-Q tried to picture it between the shelter posts. The long table had wide legs and a wobbly foot. Turning it through the narrow opening would take everyone.

He looked back at the timetable. Drinks should have started by now. He could hear ice ticking softly against the side of the cooler.

“I thought I could fix it before anyone noticed,” Bark-B-Q said.

Coop was still trying to reach her cup. Hen-Berry had found a patch of shade for the salad. Leo was holding the cloth down with both paws.

Bark-B-Q took the pencil from behind his ear.

“What would make lunch work for you?”

“A chair I can pull out,” said Hen-Berry.

“A table where I can reach things,” said Coop.

“A place to put the cold jug,” said Leo. “I’ve got a folding table in my camp trailer. It’s a little shorter than this one. Want to see if it fits?”

Bark-B-Q put his timetable down. “Yes, please.”

Leo came back carrying the table by its handle, with the legs folded flat beneath it. Eggs-Benedict stretched a piece of spare cord between the shelter posts. Coop held one end while Eggs pinched the cord at the other post.

They held the cord against the long edge of the table. The cord was a good wingtip longer. The table would fit.

The table cleared the posts. Leo and Bark-B-Q unfolded the legs and set it down in the shade. It stood steady on the shelter floor with room to walk all the way round.

“Smaller table,” said Eggs-Benedict. “Same number of friends.”

Panda brought up the little chairs that had been stacked at the back of the shelter.

Bark-B-Q started to gather up the place cards, then put them down again. “Could someone bring these in? I’ll check the food.”

“We’ve got them,” said Hen-Berry. She lifted the salad dish while Cluck and Coop collected the cards.

Cluck held the two cards marked with a watch and a star together like a pair of tickets.

This time Coop chose a low chair with a firm cushion and put her cup where she could reach it. Hen-Berry pulled out a chair with no rail in her way. Leo brought over Bark-B-Q’s blue chair and kept the passage clear.

Bark-B-Q caught himself straightening three plates in a row. Then he passed the rest to Hen-Berry.
